games.title: Cells or No Cells?
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about which things are made of cells. A cell is the smallest living piece of a living thing. Players sort each card: made of living cells now, made of cells that were once alive, or never made of cells.

printables.title: 27 thing cards to cut out
items: A mango leaf on the tree
A dry leaf on the ground
Green slime on a water tank
A chicken egg from a shop
TEST IT: look at your fingertip with a magnifier. Can you see the cells? Why not?
TEST IT: look at a grain of salt with a magnifier. Is it made of cells, or of something else?
TEST IT: tear a piece of paper and look at the torn edge with a magnifier. What do you see?

rules: Cut out the 27 cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
On your turn, take the top card and read it out loud.
Put it on one mat: LIVING CELLS NOW, CELLS THAT WERE ONCE ALIVE, or NEVER MADE OF CELLS. Say why.
If the others agree, win one cell token. If someone disagrees, both of you give a reason, and the group decides.
If you draw a TEST IT card, everyone does the test. The first one to explain the result wins two tokens.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins.

setup.art: Three paper mats on a floor, one with a green sprouting leaf, one with a wooden spoon, one with a stone, and a pile of face-down cards.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats. Put the cards face down.

setup.art: A child holding a card showing a wooden spoon, pointing at the middle mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Put it on a mat and say why.

setup.art: Children looking at a fingertip and a grain of salt through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 3. TEST IT cards: everyone tries the test.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor. 2. Shuffle the cards and put them face down. 3. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every living thing is made of tiny living pieces called cells. Some things were made by cells long ago, but are not alive now. Some things were never made of cells at all. Let's sort them.
flow.kid: Put the three mats down. Mix the cards. For each card, decide. Living cells now? Cells that were once alive? Or never cells?
flow.context: This is the first step of Cells or No Cells?, a sorting card game. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the card 'A wooden spoon'. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. A wooden spoon. Is it alive? Was it ever made by living cells?
flow.kid: Practice card: a wooden spoon. Which mat does it go on?

ask.q: Where did the wood come from?
good: A tree was alive, and wood is made of its cells' walls.

check.why: Wood comes from a tree. It is made of the stiff walls of tree cells, which are now dead. So it was made by living cells, but it is not alive now. Picking 'never made of cells' usually means thinking anything hard and still is like a stone. Picking 'living cells now' usually means thinking anything from a tree is still alive.

flow.do: Take turns drawing cards until all are sorted. Do each TEST IT card together when it comes up.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card, choose a mat, and give your reason.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Choose a mat. Say why.
flow.parent: Tricky cards: a cloud and a candle flame were never made of cells, even though clouds grow and flames use up fuel. Curd and risen dosa batter hold living bacteria and yeast cells. A pearl is made by an oyster, but it is hard mineral layers that the oyster's cells laid down, not cells, so it goes in 'never made of cells'. The hair you can see is made of cells that have died, so it goes in 'once alive'. The yolk of a shop egg began as one huge cell from the hen. Accept 'living cells now' or 'once alive' if your child gives a reason.

check.q: Curd from the kitchen. Which mat?
check.why: Curd is milk that has been changed by bacteria. Bacteria are tiny single cells, and in fresh curd millions of them are alive. That is why a spoonful of curd can set a new bowl of milk. Picking 'never made of cells' usually means thinking curd is only milk.

flow.do: When a TEST IT card comes up, everyone does the test.
flow.say: Look at your fingertip with the magnifier. Can you see cells? Why do you think not?
flow.kid: Look at your fingertip with the magnifier. Can you see cells?

ask.q: Why can't we see cells on our fingertip with a magnifier?
good: The magnifier is not strong enough.
There are too many layers on top of each other.

check.q: A grain of salt under the magnifier looks like a little cube. Is the cube a cell?
options: Yes, it is one big cell
No, salt was never alive, so it has no cells
Yes, all small things are cells
check.why: Salt is a crystal. It forms when salty water dries. It was never alive, so it has no cells. Its straight edges come from its tiny particles lining up in rows. Picking 'one big cell' usually means mixing up any small neat shape with a cell.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then look at each mat together.
flow.say: Look at the 'once alive' mat. Which card surprised you most?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Look at the 'once alive' mat. Which card surprised you?
flow.think: Is there any card you still are not sure about? How could you find out?

games.title: Run and Tumble: be a bacterium
games.players: 2 or more: one 'bacterium' and one 'food maker'
games.context: This is a moving game. A real bacterium has no eyes and no brain. It senses the chemicals of food in the water, a little like smelling. It swims straight, then checks: is the smell stronger now than a moment ago? If yes, it keeps going. If no, it tumbles and picks a new direction. You play the bacterium.
rules: One player is the bacterium. They close their eyes or wear a loose cloth over them.
The food maker hides a piece of food, like a cut lemon or a sweet, somewhere in the room.
The bacterium takes 3 steps forward in a straight line. This is a 'run'.
After each run, the food maker says 'stronger' if the bacterium is closer to the food than before, or 'weaker' if it is further away.
If it is stronger, the bacterium runs again the same way. If it is weaker, the bacterium tumbles: it spins slowly on the spot, stops, and sets off facing a new way.
Count the runs it takes to touch the food. Then swap.

setup.art: A child with a soft cloth over their eyes standing in a cleared room, a cut lemon on a stool in the corner.
setup.caption: 1. Clear the floor. Hide the food. Cover the bacterium's eyes.

setup.art: A child taking three straight steps, with footprints, and another child saying 'stronger'.
setup.caption: 2. Run 3 steps. The food maker says stronger or weaker.

setup.art: A child spinning slowly on the spot with arms tucked in, curved arrows around them.
setup.caption: 3. Weaker? Tumble: spin round and set off a new way.

flow.do: 1. Clear a space with nothing to trip on. 2. Hide the food somewhere at floor or table height. 3. Gently cover the bacterium's eyes, or ask them to keep them shut.
flow.say: A bacterium is one tiny cell. It has no eyes and no brain. Yet it finds food. Let's find out how, by being one.
flow.kid: You are a bacterium. You are one cell. You have no eyes. Can you find the food?
flow.parent: Move chairs and sharp corners away, and walk beside the child. A slow spin is enough for the tumble.
flow.context: This is the first step of Run and Tumble, a game where a child acts out how a bacterium finds food.

flow.do: Play the game. After each 3-step run, say 'stronger' or 'weaker'. Count the runs.
flow.say: Run 3 steps. Stronger or weaker? Remember what it was a moment ago.
flow.kid: Take 3 steps. Listen. Stronger? Keep going. Weaker? Spin and try a new way.

ask.q: To know if the smell is stronger, what does the bacterium have to remember?
good: What it smelled a moment ago.

check.q: A bacterium runs, and the food smell gets weaker. What does it do?
options: Keeps going the same way, faster
Tumbles and sets off in a new direction
check.why: If the smell is weaker, the bacterium is going the wrong way. So it tumbles and tries a new direction. Picking 'keep going faster' usually means thinking bacteria always swim straight. Real E. coli bacteria run for about a second, then check and tumble if things got worse.

flow.do: Play twice more. Write the number of runs each time on the score sheet.
flow.say: Did you get better? Why might the bacterium sometimes take a long time?
flow.kid: Play again. Count your runs. Did you get faster?
flow.think: The bacterium only remembers a few seconds back. Would a longer memory help it?

flow.do: Ask your child to say three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now about how a bacterium finds food? What happened in our game that shows it? Why does it work?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: 'I think a bacterium finds food by checking if the smell is getting stronger. I saw that I reached the lemon in 6 runs, even with my eyes shut. It works because each time it got weaker I turned, so I kept the good directions.'

experiments.title: Onion Skin: is an onion made of tiny rooms?
experiments.context: In this experiment you peel the very thin skin from inside an onion layer and look at it with stronger and stronger magnifiers. You find out whether an onion is made of cells, the tiny living pieces of living things.
experiments.question: Is an onion one smooth thing, or is it made of tiny pieces?
experiments.predict: Before you look, draw what you think you will see when the onion skin is made 10 times bigger, and say why you think so. Then draw what you think you will see at 100 times bigger.
experiments.fair_test: Look at the same piece of onion skin with each tool, in the same light, so only the magnifier changes. Look for at least one minute with each, because eyes take time to settle.
results_table: How much bigger it makes things
Could I see separate boxes? (yes or no)

materials.item: one onion
a toothpick, to smooth out folds
a strip of clear plastic from a packet, or a glass slide
water and a dropper, or a straw
a stain: a drop of brown iodine antiseptic (povidone-iodine) from the first-aid box, or blue fountain-pen ink if you have it
a phone with a camera, for the water-drop lens (activity a2). A hand lens helps too. A Foldscope or toy microscope shows the most, if you have one.
a bright window or a torch

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the onion. Iodine stains skin and cloth and must not be swallowed, so a grown-up adds it. Keep water off the phone's charging point. Wash hands after.

schedule.what: Peel onion skin, look with each magnifier, stain it, and draw what you see.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the onion skin at the strongest magnification you have. Label one cell, one wall and, if you saw one, a nucleus.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands breaking a fresh onion layer, and a child pulling off the thin see-through skin from its inside with fingertips.
setup.caption: 1. Break an onion layer. Peel the thin skin from its inside.

setup.art: The thin onion skin laid flat on a glass slide with one drop of water on it.
setup.caption: 2. Lay it flat on a slide or clear plastic. Add one drop of water.

setup.art: A child holding a phone, with a tiny water drop on its camera lens, very close to an onion skin on clear plastic held against a window. A zoomed circle shows faint brick-shaped cells.
setup.caption: 3. Look with each magnifier. Then add a drop of stain and look again.

flow.do: Show your child a whole onion. Cut it in half. Let them feel a layer.
flow.say: This onion looks like one smooth thing. Is it? Or is it made of tiny pieces we cannot see? What do you think?
flow.kid: Look at the onion. Feel a layer. Is it one smooth thing, or made of tiny pieces? Draw your guess.

ask.q: What do you think the onion is made of, if we zoom in?
good: I don't know, let's find out.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Onion Skin experiment. You guess what an onion looks like up close.

flow.do: 1. Snap one layer of onion backwards. 2. A thin, see-through skin hangs from the inside. Pull off a piece about the size of a stamp. 3. Lay it flat on the slide. 4. Add one drop of water. Smooth out any folds with a toothpick.
flow.say: This skin is so thin you can see your finger through it. It is only one cell thick. Let's lay it flat.
flow.kid: Snap the onion layer. Pull off the thin see-through skin. Lay it flat on the slide. Add one drop of water.
flow.parent: If the skin folds, float it in a little water and lift it out flat. Bubbles look like black-edged circles. They are not cells.

flow.do: 1. Look at the skin with your eyes alone, then with a hand lens if you have one. 2. Put a tiny drop of water, the size of a mustard seed, on the phone's main camera lens. 3. Hold the onion skin against a bright window, or over a torch. 4. Bring the phone's lens very close, about 2 to 3 millimetres from the skin, without letting the drop touch it. Tap the screen to focus, and take a photo. 5. Zoom in on the photo.
flow.say: What changes as we use a stronger lens? When do you first see separate shapes?
flow.kid: Look with just your eyes. Then use the phone with a water drop. Hold the skin up to the light. When do you first see shapes?
flow.parent: What to expect. With eyes alone or a hand lens, you will see a clear sheet, perhaps with faint lines. With the phone and a water drop, you will usually see faint, blurry rows of long boxes. It can take several tries. If it stays blurry, move the phone a little closer or further away, use a smaller drop, put more light behind the skin, and hold the phone very still. Use the main camera at normal zoom, because some phones switch to another lens when you zoom in. A Foldscope or toy microscope shows the boxes clearly.

check.q: Under a strong lens, the onion skin shows long boxes fitted side by side. What are they?
options: Cells, the tiny living pieces the onion is made of
check.why: The boxes are onion cells. Each one is a living cell with a wall around it. Air bubbles look like round circles with thick dark edges, and they move. Scratches stay still when you move the onion skin. Picking 'bubbles' is common, because bubbles are the first thing many people notice.

flow.do: A grown-up puts one drop of iodine antiseptic or blue ink on the skin. Wait one minute. Gently dab off the extra with tissue. Look again.
flow.say: The stain colours the cells. Look again. Do the boxes show up better now? Can you see a dot inside any of them?
flow.kid: A grown-up adds one drop of colour. Wait a minute. Look again. Can you see a dark dot inside a box?
flow.parent: The stain makes the cells' edges darker. The dark dot, the nucleus, is often too small for a phone and water drop. That is normal. A Foldscope or microscope shows it.

flow.do: Your child draws one patch of cells, as big as a page. Label a cell and a wall, and a nucleus if you saw one.
flow.say: Draw what you see, not what you think you should see. Make it big.
flow.kid: Draw what you see. Make it big. Label one cell and one wall.
flow.think: Every onion in the market is built of these. How many cells do you think are in a whole onion?

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: Now tell me three things. What do you think an onion is made of? What did you see that shows it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: 'I think an onion is made of tiny cells. With the phone and a water drop, I saw long boxes side by side. The onion is made of many small living parts, like a wall made of bricks.'

experiments.title: Cheek Cells: are you made of tiny rooms too?
experiments.context: In this experiment you gently scrape the inside of your own cheek and look at the cells. You need a Foldscope, or a toy or school microscope. A phone with a water drop is not strong enough to show their shape. Then you compare your cells with onion cells.
experiments.question: Are my cells like onion cells, or different?
experiments.predict: Draw what you think your cheek cells will look like. Will they be boxes, like onion cells? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same stain, the same slide and the same magnifier as for the onion. Then any difference comes from the cells, not the tools.

materials.item: a new, clean flat ice-cream stick, or the handle of a clean steel spoon
a glass slide and a coverslip, or two small squares of clear plastic
a drop of blue fountain-pen ink, or methylene blue from a chemist or an aquarium shop
a Foldscope, or a toy or school microscope. A hand lens or a phone with a water drop will not show cheek cells.
your onion drawing from experiment e1

experiments.safety: Scrape gently, only your own cheek, with a new stick. Never share sticks. Throw them away and wash your hands after.

schedule.what: Scrape cheek cells, stain them, look, draw, and compare with the onion.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with rows for shape, edges, the dark dot and colour. Draw a cheek cell next to an onion cell.

setup.art: A child gently rubbing the inside of their cheek with the flat end of a clean ice-cream stick.
setup.caption: 1. Gently scrape the inside of your cheek with a clean stick.

setup.art: The stick being smeared on a glass slide, and one drop of blue colour added.
setup.caption: 2. Smear it on a slide. Add one drop of colour.

setup.art: A child at a small microscope, and a zoomed circle showing blue fried-egg-shaped cells.
setup.caption: 3. Look through the microscope. Compare with your onion drawing.

flow.do: Show your child their onion drawing. Hand them a new, clean stick.
flow.say: Your onion was made of cells. Are you? Let's look at the inside of your cheek. It sheds old cells all the time, and a gentle scrape just collects some. It doesn't hurt.
flow.kid: Remember the onion cells? Now let's look at you. The inside of your cheek is always shedding cells.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Cheek Cells experiment. You will look at your own cells.

flow.do: 1. Your child gently rubs the flat end of the stick on the inside of their cheek, 5 times. 2. They smear the stick on the middle of the slide. 3. Add one drop of colour. 4. Put a coverslip or plastic square on top.
flow.say: Gently, like stroking a cat. Five times. Now smear it on the glass.
flow.kid: Rub the stick gently inside your cheek, 5 times. Smear it on the slide. Add one drop of colour.
flow.parent: The smear will look like almost nothing. That is normal: there are thousands of cells in it.

flow.do: Look through the microscope or Foldscope. Start with the weakest lens. Move the slide slowly to find blue patches.
flow.say: Look for flat shapes like fried eggs. Can you find a dark yolk in one?
flow.kid: Look for flat blue shapes. They might be folded. Find a dark dot in one.

check.q: How are your cheek cells different from onion cells?
options: They are soft, flat and round-ish, with no stiff wall
They are exactly the same long boxes
They have no nucleus at all
check.why: Cheek cells are animal cells. They have no cell wall, so they are floppy, flat and roundish, often folded. Onion cells are plant cells with stiff walls, so they look like boxes. Both have a nucleus, the dark dot. Picking 'exactly the same' usually means the cells were too faint to see clearly. Try more stain or more light.

flow.parent: Cheek cells are clear and thin, so they are hard to find. Use the stain and plenty of light. If you have no microscope, still make the smear. The faint blue haze on the slide is thousands of your cells. Then look at the third step picture to see their shape.

flow.do: Your child draws a cheek cell next to an onion cell and fills in the table.
flow.say: What is the same about your cells and the onion's? What is different?
flow.kid: Draw your cell next to an onion cell. What is the same? What is different?

good: Onion cells are boxes, mine are floppy.

flow.do: Ask your child for three sentences: what I think, what I saw, why.
flow.say: What do you think now? What did you see? Why do you think plant cells and your cells look different?
flow.kid: What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: 'I think I am made of cells like the onion. I saw flat blue cells with dark dots. They were not boxes because my cells have no walls, but onion cells do, to help the plant stand up.'

experiments.title: Curd Bowls: does milk need living cells to become curd?
experiments.context: In this experiment you set three bowls of warm milk overnight: one with living curd, one with nothing, and one with curd that was boiled first. You find out whether curd is made by living cells. If you did the Habitats bowls, those asked where curd sets best: warm, on the counter or in the fridge. These bowls ask a different question: can boiled curd still set milk, or only living curd?
experiments.question: Will boiled curd still turn warm milk into curd?
experiments.predict: Which of the three bowls do you think will turn into curd by morning? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same milk, the same amount in each bowl, and the same warm place for the same time. Only change what you add. Use a clean spoon for each bowl, so no living curd gets into bowl C by mistake.

materials.item: milk, boiled and cooled until lukewarm
materials.qty: about one and a half cups

materials.item: plain curd, home-set or from a shop
3 small steel katoris or bowls, with plates to cover them
a small steel vessel and the stove, for boiling one spoon of curd (grown-up only)
tape and a pen, to label the bowls A, B and C, and 3 clean spoons

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils the milk and the curd. Hot milk burns. Bowl A is ordinary curd and can be eaten. Pour bowls B and C away.

schedule.what: Boil one spoon of curd. Set up three bowls of lukewarm milk: A with living curd, B with nothing, C with the boiled curd. Boil the milk earlier, so it has time to cool.
Check the three bowls. Fill in the table. Say what you think, what you saw, and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all three bowls. Draw each bowl, tilted, to show if it is thick or runny.

setup.art: A grown-up stirring one spoon of curd in a small steel vessel on a low flame until it bubbles.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils one spoon of curd, then lets it cool.

setup.art: Three steel katoris labelled A, B and C with lukewarm milk: a spoon of curd going into A, nothing into B, the boiled curd into C.
setup.caption: 2. Lukewarm milk in three bowls. A gets living curd, B gets nothing, C gets the boiled curd.

setup.art: Next morning, three tilted katoris: A thick and set, B and C still runny.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, tilt each bowl. Which ones set?

flow.context: This is the first step of the Curd Bowls experiment. You think about why we add old curd to milk.
flow.do: Show your child a bowl of curd and a cup of milk.
flow.say: To make curd, we stir a spoon of old curd into warm milk. Why do you think we need the old curd? What do you think is in it?
flow.kid: Look at the curd and the milk. We add old curd to milk to make curd. Why? What is in it?

ask.q: What do you think is in the old curd that turns milk into curd?
good: I don't know, let's find out.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up puts 1 spoon of curd in a small steel vessel. 2. Heat it on a low flame, stirring, until it bubbles, and let it bubble for half a minute. 3. Let it cool for a few minutes. 4. Label three bowls A, B and C with tape.
flow.say: I am boiling this spoon of curd. Do you think boiled curd can still turn milk into curd? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A grown-up boils one spoon of curd. Then it cools. Can boiled curd still make curd? Why do you think so?
flow.parent: Boiled curd splits into lumps and watery whey. That is fine. Let it cool before it goes into the milk. If you did the three bowls in the Habitats unit, tell your child this test is different: there, every bowl got living curd and only the place changed. Here, every bowl is in the same place and only the curd changes.

flow.do: 1. Pour the lukewarm milk into the three bowls, about half a cup each. 2. Bowl A: stir in 1 spoon of curd with a clean spoon. 3. Bowl B: add nothing. 4. Bowl C: stir in the boiled curd with another clean spoon. 5. Cover all three, and keep them together in a warm place overnight.
flow.say: Each bowl gets the same milk, in the same place, for the same time. Only one thing changes: what we add.
flow.kid: Pour milk into the three bowls. Add curd to A. Add nothing to B. Add the boiled curd to C. Use a clean spoon each time. Cover them.
flow.parent: The milk should feel warm but not hot on the inside of your wrist. Hot milk kills curd bacteria, and cold milk sets very slowly. In cold weather, wrap the bowls in a towel or keep them in a closed cupboard. They may need 10 hours or more.

flow.wait: Leave the bowls overnight, or for 6 to 10 hours.
flow.do: Next morning, tilt each bowl gently. Write in the table whether it is thick or runny, and how it smells.
flow.say: Which bowls set? Is that what you guessed?
flow.kid: Tilt each bowl slowly. Is it thick or runny? Smell it. Write it down.
flow.parent: What to expect: bowl A is thick curd. Bowls B and C stay runny. In hot weather, B and C may turn a little sour or lumpy after a day, from a few bacteria that got in from the air. If you have a Foldscope or microscope, look at a tiny dab of bowl A in a drop of water. You may see tiny rods and dots: curd bacteria.

check.q: Bowl A, with living curd, set into curd. Bowl C, with boiled curd, stayed runny. Why?
options: Heat killed the bacteria in the curd, so there were no living cells to multiply
Boiled curd is too lumpy to mix with milk
check.why: Curd is set by living bacteria. In warm milk they split again and again, and turn the milk sour and thick. Boiling killed them, so nothing could multiply in bowl C. Bowl B had no curd bacteria added at all. Picking 'unlucky' is worth testing: do it again and see if the same thing happens.

flow.do: Ask your child to say three things: what they think, what they saw, and why.
flow.say: What do you think turns milk into curd? What did you see in our three bowls that shows it? Why did bowl C stay runny?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: 'I think living bacteria in curd turn milk into curd. Bowl A set, but bowl B and bowl C stayed runny. Boiling killed the bacteria in C, so there were no living cells to make more cells.'

activities.title: Zoom Walk: what do things look like up close?
activities.context: This is a short noticing walk around the home. You look at ordinary things with your eyes, then with a magnifier, and notice which ones show tiny repeating patterns.

materials.item: a magnifying glass or a phone camera zoomed in
paper and a pencil

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun through a magnifier. It can burn your eyes.

schedule.what: Look at 8 things up close. Notice and wonder.

activities.record: Draw 4 of the things, once as your eye sees them and once as the magnifier shows them.

setup.art: A tray with a leaf, a pinch of salt, a strip of cloth, a strand of hair, a piece of paper and a slice of tomato.
setup.caption: 1. Gather 8 things on a tray.

setup.art: A child holding a magnifying glass over a green leaf, with the leaf's veins looking huge.
setup.caption: 2. Look at each with your eyes, then with the magnifier.

setup.art: A child's drawing split in two: a leaf as seen by eye, and the same leaf with net-like lines up close.
setup.caption: 3. Draw what changes. Say what you notice and wonder.

flow.do: Put 8 things on a tray: a leaf, a pinch of salt, a pinch of sugar and a piece of cloth. Add a strand of hair, a piece of paper and a slice of tomato. The eighth thing is your own fingertip.
flow.say: We're going to be zoom explorers. First, just look with your eyes. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Look at each thing with just your eyes. What do you notice?
flow.context: This is the first step of the Zoom Walk. You look closely at ordinary things before learning about cells.

flow.do: Look at each thing with the magnifier. Take turns saying one thing you notice and one thing you wonder.
flow.say: What do you notice now? What do you wonder?
flow.kid: Look with the magnifier. Say one thing you notice. Say one thing you wonder.
flow.parent: Good things to hear: the leaf has a net of lines, the tomato has tiny shiny bags, salt is little cubes, the cloth is woven threads. Don't explain cells yet. Just collect wonderings.

ask.q: Which things look like they are made of tiny pieces?

flow.do: Your child draws 4 things, by eye and by magnifier.
flow.say: Which of these were once alive? Do they look different up close from the things that were never alive?
flow.kid: Draw 4 things, by eye and up close. Which ones were once alive?
flow.think: What do you think you would see if you zoomed in even more, 100 times more?

activities.title: Make a Water-Drop Magnifier
activities.context: In this activity you make a lens from one drop of water. A round drop bends light, so things under it look bigger. Leeuwenhoek's lenses were tiny glass beads that worked in the same way.

materials.item: a strip of clear plastic from a packet, or a clear plastic lid
water and a dropper or a straw
a newspaper
a phone with a camera (optional)

activities.safety: Keep water away from plugs and switches. Wipe the phone lens dry after.

schedule.what: Make a water-drop lens. Test it on newspaper. Try it on the phone camera.

activities.record: Write down which drop made the letters biggest: a small drop or a big drop.

setup.art: A dropper putting one round drop of water on a strip of clear plastic held over newspaper.
setup.caption: 1. Put one drop of water on clear plastic.

setup.art: The same plastic held just above newspaper, one letter under the drop looking much bigger.
setup.caption: 2. Hold it just above newspaper. Move it up and down until the letters are clear.

setup.art: A tiny drop of water sitting right on the camera lens of a phone, which shows a giant close-up of a leaf.
setup.caption: 3. With a grown-up, put a tiny drop on a phone camera lens and look close up.

flow.do: 1. Put a small drop of water on the plastic. 2. Lay the plastic on the newspaper, with the drop over a letter. 3. Lift the plastic slowly, a few millimetres at a time, and watch the letter.
flow.say: Look at the letter under the drop. What happens to it?
flow.kid: Put one drop of water on the plastic. Hold it over a newspaper. What happens to the letters?
flow.context: This is the first step of making a water-drop magnifier. You turn a drop of water into a lens.

flow.do: Try a big flat drop and a tiny round drop. Compare them.
flow.say: Which makes letters bigger: the big flat drop or the tiny round one? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Try a big drop and a tiny drop. Which makes letters bigger?

check.q: Which drop makes letters look bigger?
check.why: A tiny drop is more curved. The more curved a lens is, the more it bends light, and the bigger things look. That is why Leeuwenhoek's best lenses were tiny glass beads. Picking 'the big drop' usually means thinking a bigger lens always magnifies more. A big lens shows more, but a curvier lens magnifies more.

flow.do: With a grown-up, put one tiny drop of water right on the phone's main camera lens. Turn the phone over carefully and open the camera. Hold it 2 to 3 millimetres from a leaf or onion skin, without touching it.
flow.say: Our phone is now a microscope! What can you see that you couldn't before?
flow.kid: With a grown-up, put a tiny drop on the phone camera. Look at a leaf very close.
flow.parent: Hold the phone lens-up while adding the drop, then turn it over gently. A drop the size of a mustard seed clings best. Tap to focus. Phone cameras differ, and some stay blurry. Wipe the lens dry afterwards.

flow.do: Ask your child why a drop of water makes things bigger.
flow.say: Why do you think a drop of water can be a lens?
flow.kid: Why does a drop of water make things look bigger?

good: It is clear and round like a lens.

activities.title: The Size Ladder: from you to a cell
activities.context: In this activity you make a paper ladder of sizes. Each step down is 10 times smaller than the one above. It shows how tiny a cell is compared with you.

materials.item: a long strip of paper, about 1 metre, or newspaper sheets taped together
a ruler
a mustard seed, an ant or a picture of one, and a leaf
pencils or crayons

activities.safety: No safety worries. If you look at a real ant, let it go afterwards.

schedule.what: Make the size ladder with 7 steps, from you to a bacterium.

activities.record: Your ladder has 7 steps. Under each, write how big it is.

setup.art: A child lying next to a long paper strip with a line drawn at their height of about 1 metre.
setup.caption: 1. Step 1: you, about 1 metre.

setup.art: A paper strip with drawn steps: a hand, a big ant, a mustard seed, each ten times smaller.
setup.caption: 2. Each step is 10 times smaller: 10 cm, 1 cm, 1 mm.

setup.art: The bottom of the ladder with tiny dots labelled onion cell, red blood cell and bacterium, and a magnifier over them.
setup.caption: 3. Then cells: 0.1 mm, 0.01 mm and 0.001 mm.

flow.do: Draw seven boxes down the paper strip. In box 1, draw your child. Write 'about 1 metre'.
flow.say: We're going down a ladder. Each step is 10 times smaller than the last. Step one is you.
flow.kid: Draw 7 boxes. In box 1, draw yourself. Write: about 1 metre.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Size Ladder. You build a ladder of sizes, from you down to a cell.

flow.do: Fill in boxes 2 to 4 together: a hand (10 centimetres), a big black ant (1 centimetre), a mustard seed (1 millimetre). Use the ruler to check each.
flow.say: Ten of your hands would stretch about as tall as you. Ten big ants would line up along your hand. Ten mustard seeds would line up along a big ant.
flow.kid: Box 2: a hand, 10 cm. Box 3: a big ant, 1 cm. Box 4: a mustard seed, 1 mm.

ask.q: How many big ants would fit along your hand?

flow.do: Fill in boxes 5 to 7: an onion cell (a tenth of a millimetre), a red blood cell (a hundredth of a millimetre), a bacterium (a thousandth of a millimetre).
flow.say: From here on, things are too small to see clearly without a lens. Ten onion cells fit along a mustard seed. Your cheek cells fit between box 5 and box 6.
flow.kid: Box 5: an onion cell. Box 6: a red blood cell. Box 7: a bacterium.

check.q: About how many onion cells fit side by side across one mustard seed?
check.why: A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre across. An onion cell is about a tenth of a millimetre wide. So about 10 fit across. Picking '1' usually means thinking cells are as big as seeds. Picking 'a million' is too many for one row, though a whole onion has millions of cells.

flow.do: Ask your child where on the ladder their eyes stop seeing.
flow.say: Where does your eye stop being able to see? What do we need below that step?
flow.kid: Point to where your eyes stop seeing. What do you need below that?
flow.think: Bacteria are on the last step. Are there living things even smaller?

activities.title: Draw What's Inside You: before and after
activities.context: In this activity you draw what you think you are made of, deep inside, before you learn about cells. At the end of the unit you draw it again and compare. Scientists use drawings like these as models.

materials.item: two sheets of paper and crayons

schedule.what: Draw what you think is inside you, as deep as you can imagine.
After seeing cells, draw it again. Compare the two drawings.

activities.record: Keep both drawings side by side, with the dates.

setup.art: A child drawing an outline of their own body on paper, with question marks inside.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the outline of your body.

setup.art: The same outline filled with bones, a heart and a zoomed-in circle that is still empty.
setup.caption: 2. Draw what is inside, as deep as you can imagine.

setup.art: Two drawings side by side, the second with a zoomed circle full of tiny cells.
setup.caption: 3. After the unit, draw again. Compare.

flow.do: Your child draws an outline of their body and fills in what they think is inside. Add a zoom circle: 'If we zoomed into my finger, what would we see?'
flow.say: Draw what you think you are made of. Go as deep as you can. What is under your skin? What is under that?
flow.kid: Draw yourself. Fill in what is inside. Draw a zoom circle on your finger. What is in there?
flow.context: This is the first step of Draw What's Inside You. You draw your idea before learning about cells.
flow.parent: Do not correct anything. This drawing shows your child's starting idea.

flow.do: After experiments e1 and e2, your child draws again and compares the two drawings.
flow.say: What is new in your second drawing? What changed your mind?
flow.kid: Draw yourself again. What is new? What changed your mind?
flow.wait: Do this after the cell experiments.

good: The zoom circle has tiny rooms now.
Everything is made of cells, even bones.

activities.title: Cells You Can Almost See: tomato, cotton and leaf peel
activities.context: Some cells are big enough to see with just a hand lens. In this activity you look at the juicy cells of a tomato, a single long cotton cell, and the purple cells peeled from a leaf.

materials.item: a ripe tomato or a piece of watermelon
a little cotton wool
a leaf with a purple underside, like Rhoeo (Moses-in-the-cradle), if you have one, or any soft leaf
a hand lens, or a phone with a water-drop lens
a dark sheet of paper

activities.safety: A grown-up cuts the tomato. Wash hands after.

schedule.what: Look at tomato pulp, cotton and leaf peel up close. Draw each.

activities.record: Draw the three kinds of cells. Write one word for each shape.

setup.art: A spoonful of ripe tomato pulp spread on a white plate, with a hand lens showing shiny round bags.
setup.caption: 1. Spread a little tomato pulp. Look for shiny bags.

setup.art: A single cotton fibre pulled from cotton wool, laid on dark paper under a lens.
setup.caption: 2. Pull one cotton fibre. Lay it on dark paper.

setup.art: Fingers tearing a purple leaf at an angle, and a thin purple strip peeling off.
setup.caption: 3. Tear a leaf at a slant to peel off a thin skin.

flow.do: Spread a little ripe tomato pulp on a plate. Look with the hand lens.
flow.say: See those shiny little bags? Each one is a single tomato cell, full of juice.
flow.kid: Look at the tomato pulp. Can you see tiny shiny bags? Each one is a cell!
flow.context: This is the first step of Cells You Can Almost See. Some fruit cells are big enough to see with a hand lens.

flow.do: Pull one single fibre from the cotton wool. Lay it on the dark paper and look with the lens.
flow.say: This whole thread is just one cell. Cotton plants grow these long cells on their seeds.
flow.kid: Pull out one cotton fibre, a single hair of cotton. Look at it. The whole fibre is one cell!

options: made of thousands of round cells
not made of cells at all
check.why: Each cotton fibre grows from one cell on the cotton seed's skin. The cell grows very long, then dies, leaving its tube-shaped wall. Picking 'not made of cells' usually means thinking cloth was never alive. Cotton comes from a plant.

flow.do: Tear the leaf at a slant so a thin, coloured skin peels off. Lay it on a slide or plate with a drop of water. Look with the strongest lens you have.
flow.say: Do you see little shapes fitted together? Leaves also have tiny paired openings, called stomata, that let air in. You need a microscope to see those.
flow.kid: Tear the leaf at a slant. Find the thin skin. Look closely. Do you see shapes fitted together?
flow.parent: With a hand lens you will see only the leaf's colour and veins. A phone with a water drop may show a faint pattern of shapes, best on a purple Rhoeo peel. Stomata need a Foldscope or microscope.

flow.do: Lay out the three drawings side by side.
flow.say: Which cells were round? Which were long? Which were like tiles?
flow.kid: Look at your three drawings. Round, long or tiles?
flow.think: Why might a tomato cell be round and juicy, but a cotton cell long and thin?

projects.title: My Cell Atlas: a week of looking
projects.context: In this project you make your own little book of cells. Over five days you look at a new living thing each day, draw or photograph its cells, and write one fact.

materials.item: a notebook or 6 sheets of paper stapled together
a Foldscope, toy microscope, or phone with a water-drop lens
glass slides or clear plastic strips
things to look at: onion, a leaf, curd, a raw potato, and a jar of water with a few torn spinach or coriander leaves in it

projects.safety: A grown-up handles knives, iodine and the jar of leaf water. Wash hands after each look. Never taste the samples.

schedule.what: Make the cover. First page: onion cells. Also put a few torn spinach or coriander leaves in a jar of water, and leave it by a window for day 5.
Third page: a tiny dab of curd with a drop of water. Look for tiny rods and dots.
Fourth page: a thin slice of raw potato with a drop of iodine. The starch grains inside the cells turn dark blue-black.
Fifth page: a drop of water from the leaf jar. Last page: 'What I am made of'. Show the atlas to someone.

projects.record: Each page has a drawing or photo, the name of the living thing, the magnifier used, and one fact.

setup.art: A handmade notebook with a cover reading in pictures: a magnifier and a cell.
setup.caption: 1. Make a little book with a cover.

setup.art: A child with a phone held over a thin potato slice, a dropper beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Each day, look at one new living thing.

setup.art: An open notebook page with a drawing of cells, a label and a short fact.
setup.caption: 3. Draw or stick a photo. Write one fact.

flow.do: Make the atlas cover together. Then do the onion page, using what you learned in e1. Last, put a few torn spinach or coriander leaves in a jar of water. Cover it loosely and leave it by a window until day 5.
flow.say: Scientists keep notebooks of everything they see. This is your cell atlas. Let's start with the onion.
flow.kid: Make your atlas cover. Then draw your onion cells on page 1.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Cell Atlas, a five-day project where you collect pictures of cells.

flow.do: On day 2, peel a thin skin from a leaf. Look, draw and write.
flow.say: How are these leaf cells like the onion cells? How are they different?
flow.kid: Peel a leaf skin. Look. Draw. Write one fact.

flow.do: On day 3, put a tiny dab of curd with a drop of water on a slide. Look with the strongest lens.
flow.say: Curd is full of bacteria. They are much smaller than onion cells. Can you see tiny dots or rods?
flow.kid: Look at a tiny dab of curd. Can you find tiny dots or rods? Those are bacteria.
flow.parent: With a Foldscope you may just see tiny specks that jiggle. With a hand lens or a phone you will not see bacteria. That is a good result: it shows how tiny they are.

flow.do: On day 4, a grown-up cuts a very thin slice of raw potato and adds one drop of iodine antiseptic. Look by eye, then with your strongest lens.
flow.say: Inside potato cells are tiny grains of starch, the plant's stored food. Iodine turns starch dark blue-black. Where does the colour go?
flow.kid: A grown-up adds iodine to a potato slice. What turns dark?

check.q: The dark blue-black grains in potato cells are…
check.why: Iodine turns starch dark blue-black. Potato cells store food as tiny starch grains. Picking 'bacteria' usually means thinking anything small and dark is a germ.

flow.parent: The whole cut surface goes blue-black, which you can see by eye. A Foldscope shows the separate starch grains inside the cells.

flow.do: On day 5, put a drop of water from the leaf jar on a slide and look. Then write the last page: 'What I am made of'. Show the atlas to a family member.
flow.say: Tell someone what you discovered this week. What surprised you most?
flow.kid: Look at a drop of water from the leaf jar. Write your last page: What I am made of. Show your atlas.
flow.parent: After four days, water with rotting leaves is usually full of bacteria, and often of single cells that swim. With a Foldscope or microscope you may see them darting about. With a phone and water drop you may see only moving specks, or nothing, because they are so small. Pour the jar away and wash hands after.

challenges.title: The Best Home Microscope
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Using only things from home, make a magnifier strong enough to see onion cells.
challenges.problem: You need to see onion cells, but you have no microscope. Using things from home, make the strongest magnifier you can.
constraints: Use only things you find at home.
Test it on the same onion skin each time, so the test is fair.
It must be safe: no broken glass.
general: Put a tiny drop of water on a phone camera lens. It works like a small, strong lens.
Look through a clear glass marble held close to your eye and the onion skin. The middle is clear, the edges are blurry.
Shine a torch from below the onion skin, so light passes through it.
creative: Make a card holder with a small hole in it. Put a water drop in the hole, like Leeuwenhoek's lens in its metal plate.
Stack two magnifiers, one after the other, like the two lenses in a real microscope.
Rest the phone, with its water drop, on two stacks of books over the onion skin, with a torch shining up from below. A steady phone gives a sharper picture.
challenges.your_turn: Invent your own magnifier. Draw it, build it and test it on onion skin. Can you see the bricks?

setup.art: A table with a marble, a dropper, clear plastic, a torch and an onion skin on a slide.
setup.caption: 1. Gather things from home and an onion skin.

setup.art: A card strip with a small hole holding a drop of water, held up to an eye over an onion skin.
setup.caption: 2. Build a magnifier.

setup.art: A child looking through the homemade magnifier, a thumbs-up beside a drawing of onion bricks.
setup.caption: 3. Test it on the onion skin. Can you see cells?

flow.do: Show your child the problem and the materials.
flow.say: We have no microscope. How can we make one from things at home?
flow.kid: You have no microscope. How can you make one from things at home?
flow.context: This is the first step of The Best Home Microscope, a design challenge to see onion cells.

flow.do: Try the usual ideas and your child's own ideas. Test each on the same onion skin.
flow.say: Which one shows the most? Why?
flow.kid: Try each idea on the same onion skin. Which shows the most?

ask.q: Why is the tiny drop stronger than a big magnifying glass?

flow.do: Your child draws their best design and what it showed.
flow.say: If you had one more day, how would you make it better?
flow.kid: Draw your best magnifier and what you saw. How could you make it better?
flow.think: Leeuwenhoek never said how he made his best lenses. Why might he have kept it secret?

challenges.title: Slime Mould Railway: join the cities
challenges.context: A slime mould is one giant yellow cell with no brain. In a famous experiment, a slime mould joined oat flakes placed like cities around Tokyo in a pattern much like the real railway. In this challenge you design a network to join cities, using as little string as you can.
challenges.problem: Six 'cities' (steel cups) sit on the floor. Join them all with string, so you can travel from any city to any other, using as little string as possible.
constraints: Every city must be joined to the network.
You may add extra meeting points (a bottle cap) where strings join.
Measure the total string used, in centimetres.
materials: a ball of string or wool
pebbles or bottle caps for meeting points
general: Join each city to the next one in a ring.
Join every city to one middle point, like spokes of a wheel.
Join the closest cities first, then link the groups.
creative: Add one or two meeting points between cities. Sometimes three roads meeting at a point saves string.
Think like the slime mould: start with string everywhere, then remove the strings that are not needed.
Ask: what if one road breaks? The slime mould kept a few extra links, so the network still worked.
challenges.your_turn: Now draw your own map of six towns you know, and design a network for them. Which design used the least string?

setup.art: Six steel cups spread across a floor like cities on a map.
setup.caption: 1. Spread out 6 cups as cities.

setup.art: String running between the cups in a ring, with a measuring tape beside it.
setup.caption: 2. Join them with string. Measure the string.

setup.art: A different network with two pebbles as meeting points, using less string.
setup.caption: 3. Try new designs. Which uses the least string?

flow.do: Place the six cups across the floor, about one big step apart.
flow.say: A slime mould is one giant cell, with no brain. It was given oat flakes placed like the cities around Tokyo. It grew tubes between them, a lot like the real railway. Can we do as well?
flow.kid: Put out 6 cups. They are cities. A one-celled slime mould joined cities like these. Can you?
flow.context: This is the first step of Slime Mould Railway, a challenge to design a network like a slime mould does.

flow.do: Try three designs. Measure the string each time and write it down.
flow.say: Which design used the least string? Can you still travel from any city to any other?
flow.kid: Try 3 ways to join the cities. Measure the string each time.

check.q: A slime mould joined food in a pattern like Tokyo's railway. What does this show?
options: One cell with no brain can find good paths
check.why: The slime mould grew tubes everywhere at first. Then the tubes that carried the most flow grew thicker, and the others faded away. With no brain, one cell found a network nearly as good as the one engineers had built. There was no map in the dish: it found the paths by growing and testing. The experiment was done in 2010, long after the railway was built, so the builders did not copy it.

flow.do: Your child explains their best design, then draws their own map of six towns.
flow.say: How did you decide which strings to keep? How do you think the slime mould decided?
flow.kid: Explain your best design. Then draw six towns you know and join them.
flow.think: The slime mould has no brain. How could it still choose the best tubes?

items.p: What is a cell?
opts: The smallest living piece of a living thing
A tiny stone inside living things
items.why: A cell is the smallest piece of a living thing that is alive by itself. Picking 'battery' happens because we also say 'cell' for batteries. It is the same word with a different meaning. Picking 'a tiny stone' usually means thinking cells are dead building blocks, but each cell is alive.
items.art: A single cell drawn big, next to a battery with a question mark.

items.p: Which of these is made of cells?
items.why: A mango leaf is part of a living tree, so it is made of cells. Steel, glass and plastic were never alive, so they have no cells. Picking 'plastic' sometimes happens because plastic is made from oil, which came from ancient life. But plastic itself has no cells.

items.p: All living things are made of cells.
items.why: True. Every living thing ever studied, from bacteria to banyan trees, is made of one or more cells.

items.p: You can see most cells with just your eyes.
items.why: False. Most cells are too small to see without a lens. A few, like a cotton fibre or a tomato cell, are big enough to almost see.

items.p: Robert Hooke looked at cork and called the little boxes he saw ____.
items.why: Hooke named them cells in 1665, from a Latin word for a small room.

items.p: The onion skin looked like long boxes side by side. Why do onion cells have straight edges?
opts: They have a stiff cell wall
items.why: Plant cells have a stiff wall outside their membrane. The walls give them straight, box-like edges. Picking 'the stain' usually means thinking the colour changed the cell's shape. The stain only makes the walls easier to see.
items.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

items.p: Your cheek cells looked like flat, floppy fried eggs. Why are they not boxes?
opts: Animal cells have no stiff wall
They were squashed by your teeth
items.why: Animal cells, like yours, have a thin membrane but no stiff wall. So they are soft and roundish. Picking 'squashed by teeth' usually means thinking all cells start as boxes.
items.context: Remember the cheek cell experiment, where you scraped the inside of your cheek and looked at the cells?

items.p: Match each tool to what it can show.
pairs: A hand lens or a phone with a water drop
the shiny cells in tomato pulp
items.why: Each stronger lens lets us see smaller things. Cheek cells need a microscope. Tomato cells are big enough for a hand lens.

items.p: Sort these. Made of living cells now, cells that were once alive, or never made of cells?
items.why: Ants and the bacteria in curd are alive now. Wood and cotton are made of cells that died. Stones and clouds were never alive, so they never had cells.

items.p: Where do new cells come from?
opts: From food turning into cells by itself
items.why: Every new cell comes from a cell splitting into two. Picking 'mud and dust' is the old idea of spontaneous generation, which careful experiments showed is not true. Food gives cells what they need to split, but food alone never becomes a cell.

items.p: A living thing that is just one cell is called a ____-celled living thing.
items.why: Single-celled living things, like bacteria and yeast, do everything with just one cell.

items.p: A wooden spoon is alive.
items.why: False. A wooden spoon is made of the walls of tree cells that have died. It was made by living cells, but it is not alive now.

items.p: Put these in order, from BIGGEST to SMALLEST: a bacterium, a big ant, an onion cell, a mustard seed.
items.why: A big ant is about 1 centimetre. A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre. An onion cell is about a tenth of a millimetre. A bacterium is about a thousandth of a millimetre.

items.p: Draw a group of onion cells as you saw them. Label one cell, one wall and one nucleus.
items.a: Long boxes fitted side by side like bricks, each with a thin outline (the wall) and a dark dot (the nucleus).
items.why: A labelled drawing shows that you looked closely and know the parts.
items.art: An empty circle like the view through a microscope.
items.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

items.p: Why did we need a magnifier to see onion cells? Use the word 'small' or 'tiny'.
items.a: Onion cells are too small for our eyes alone. Each is about a tenth of a millimetre wide. A lens bends light so they look bigger and we can see them.
items.why: Cells are tiny. Lenses make them look bigger by bending light.
items.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

items.p: Name one way your cheek cells and onion cells are alike, and one way they are different.
items.a: Alike: both are cells and both have a nucleus, a dark dot. Different: onion cells are stiff boxes with walls, cheek cells are soft and roundish with no wall.
items.why: Comparing cells helps us see what all cells share and how plant and animal cells differ.
items.context: Remember the cheek cell experiment, where you scraped the inside of your cheek and looked at the cells?

items.p: Asha set three bowls of warm milk overnight. Bowl A had a spoon of curd. Bowl B had nothing. Bowl C had a spoon of curd that was boiled first. Only bowl A set. What is the best explanation?
opts: Living bacteria in the curd split again and again, and only bowl A had living bacteria
Curd is heavy, so it makes milk thick
Milk always turns into curd by itself overnight
Boiling made the curd too sour
items.why: Cells come only from living cells. The curd in bowl A held living bacteria, which multiplied in the warm milk. Boiling killed the bacteria in bowl C, and bowl B had none added. Picking 'milk turns into curd by itself' is like the old idea of spontaneous generation: bowl B shows it does not.
items.context: Remember the curd bowls experiment, where you set three bowls of warm milk overnight?

items.p: A bacterium swims, and the sugar smell gets weaker. What does it do next?
opts: Tumbles and tries a new direction
items.why: A bacterium compares what it smells now with a few seconds ago. If it is getting weaker, it tumbles and tries another way. Picking 'keeps swimming' misses the clever part: it remembers and compares.
items.context: Remember Run and Tumble, the game where you played a bacterium finding food with your eyes shut?

items.p: A slime mould is one giant cell, and it can find the shortest path through a maze.
items.why: True. In 2000, Toshiyuki Nakagaki and his team put a slime mould in a maze with food at two ends. It ended up as one tube along the shortest path.

items.p: Which of these is a single cell?
items.why: Each cotton fibre grows from one cell on the cotton seed. A leaf and a cockroach are made of many cells. Spider silk is made by cells but is not a cell itself. Picking 'a whole leaf' usually means thinking anything thin and flat is one cell.

items.p: Leeuwenhoek called the tiny creatures he saw in water 'animal____'.
items.why: He called them animalcules, meaning little animals. Many of them were single cells.

items.p: Match each scientist to what they found.
pairs: named cells, from looking at cork
first saw living single cells in water
said all plants and animals are made of cells
showed new cells come from cells splitting
items.why: Cell theory was built by many people, one finding at a time.

items.p: Why do cheek cells keep coming off inside your mouth?
opts: Your mouth sheds old cells and grows new ones all the time
Food scrapes off cells that never grow back
items.why: The lining of your mouth is always shedding old cells and making new ones from below. Picking 'never grow back' usually means not knowing that cells come from cells splitting, so the body can replace them.
items.context: Remember the cheek cell experiment, where you scraped the inside of your cheek and looked at the cells?

items.p: A grown-up's body is made of about 30 trillion cells.
items.why: True. A careful count in 2016 found about 30 trillion human cells in a grown-up. A child has fewer, but still many trillions.

items.p: A tiny round water drop magnified letters more than a big flat drop. Why?
opts: It is more curved, so it bends light more
items.why: The more curved a lens is, the more it bends light, and the bigger things look. Picking 'more water' usually means thinking bigger lenses always magnify more.
items.context: Remember making a water-drop magnifier on clear plastic over newspaper?

items.p: Sort these into single-celled or many-celled living things.
items: a yeast cell in idli batter
items.why: Yeast, bacteria and amoebas are each one cell. Mushrooms, worms and plants are made of many cells working together.

items.p: Your brain thinks. What is your brain made of?
opts: Cells called neurons, and other cells
items.why: Your brain is made of about 86 billion neurons and many helper cells. Thinking happens when these cells pass signals. Picking 'electricity only' is half right: signals are tiny flows of charged particles, but they happen in living cells.

items.p: Rohan said cells are like bricks that don't do anything. Give one example from this unit that shows a cell doing something.
items.a: A Stentor cell bent away, reversed its hairs, shrank and swam off when specks landed on it. Or: a bacterium swims towards food by comparing smells. Or: a slime mould found the shortest path in a maze.
items.why: Cells are alive. They sense and respond, unlike bricks.

items.p: What is the difference between a wooden spoon and a living tree? Use the word 'cells'.
items.a: Both are made of cells. The tree's cells are alive: they take in food, grow and split. The spoon's cells are dead; only their walls are left, so it cannot grow.
items.why: Being made of cells is not the same as being alive now.

items.p: Draw a size ladder with 4 steps: you, a big ant, a mustard seed and an onion cell. Write how big each is.
items.a: You: about 1 metre. Big ant: about 1 cm. Mustard seed: about 1 mm. Onion cell: about one tenth of a millimetre.
items.why: Drawing the ladder shows how many times smaller each step is.
items.art: Four empty boxes going down like stairs.
items.context: Remember the Size Ladder, where each step was 10 times smaller than the one before?

items.p: Which is the fairest way to compare magnifiers on onion skin?
opts: Use the same onion skin and the same light for every magnifier
Use a new onion for each magnifier
Use the best light for the weakest magnifier
Look for a different time with each one
items.why: To be fair, change only one thing: the magnifier. Keep the onion skin, the light and the looking time the same. Otherwise you don't know which change made the difference.
items.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

items.p: Before Remak and Virchow, some scientists thought new cells formed out of a kind of liquid, like crystals forming in salty water. What evidence shows they were wrong?
opts: Under the microscope, new cells are seen forming when one cell splits into two
Cells are too small to see
Salt water has cells in it
items.why: Remak watched cells divide in growing chick eggs and showed that new cells come from old ones. Nobody has ever seen a cell form from liquid. Picking 'crystals are alive' mixes up growing by adding on the outside with growing from inside.

items.p: Why do you think cells are so small? Why isn't an elephant one giant cell?
items.a: Food and air get into a cell through its membrane, its thin skin. In a tiny cell, everything inside is close to the membrane, so food reaches it fast. In a giant cell, the middle would be too far away to get food in time. So big living things are made of many small cells.
items.why: A small cell has a lot of membrane compared with its inside. This is one reason scientists give, though a few giant cells, like slime moulds, find clever ways around it.

items.p: A slime mould crossed a bridge covered in a harmless bitter taste. At first it went slowly. After a few days, it crossed quickly. What does this show?
opts: It learned to ignore something harmless, a simple kind of memory
items.why: In 2016, Romain Boisseau, David Vogel and Audrey Dussutour showed slime moulds 'got used to' a harmless bitter taste. Getting used to something is called habituation. It is one of the simplest kinds of learning. Picking 'grew a brain' is not possible: it stayed one cell.

items.p: Scientists agree that a bacterium thinks in the same way you do.
items.why: False. Scientists agree on what bacteria do: sense, choose and remember for a few seconds. They argue about whether to call it thinking, and nobody knows yet what a bacterium feels.

items.p: Leeuwenhoek had no university degree. People doubted him. What did he do so others would believe him? What would you do?
items.a: He wrote very careful descriptions and drawings, repeated his looks many times, and sent signed letters from respected people who had seen the creatures too. Later the Royal Society saw them for itself. I would show others how to repeat my test.
items.why: Science trusts things that other people can check for themselves.

items.p: Which is the best evidence that curd has living cells in it?
opts: A spoon of it turns warm milk into curd, but a boiled spoon of it does not
It is cold from the fridge
items.why: Living cells multiply, and heat kills them. Curd sets new milk only while its bacteria are alive. Being white, cold or sour does not show life by itself.
items.context: Remember the curd bowls experiment, where you set three bowls of warm milk overnight?

items.p: You began as one single cell. Write two things that must have happened for that one cell to become you.
items.a: The cell split into two, then four, then many, again and again. The new cells became different kinds: skin, blood, bone and nerve cells.
items.why: Growing means cells splitting and cells becoming different kinds.

items.p: Which statement is an idea that scientists are still testing, not a settled fact?
opts: The first cells began as tiny fatty bubbles holding molecules that could copy themselves
All living things are made of cells
items.why: How the first cell began is still an open question. The fatty-bubble idea is one of the best guesses. The other three have been checked by millions of observations.

items.p: The brain scientist who counted the neurons in the human brain, about 86 billion, is Suzana Herculano-____.
items.why: Suzana Herculano-Houzel, a Brazilian scientist, and her team counted brain cells in 2009, using a method her lab had invented.

items.p: A Stentor cell has no brain. When specks fell on it, it bent away, then reversed its hairs, then shrank, then swam off. Which answer best describes this?
opts: Trying different responses, one after another
Doing exactly one thing for ever
items.why: Stentor tried a series of different responses. In 2019, scientists filmed this again and found most Stentors did try different things, though not always in the same order. Picking 'pushed by the water' would not explain why it changed what it did.
items.context: Remember the story of Kavya, who dropped chalk specks onto a trumpet-shaped Stentor cell?

items.p: Think of a thermostat, the switch that turns off a water heater when it is hot. It senses heat and acts. Is it thinking? How is it different from a bacterium?
items.a: A thermostat senses and acts, but it was built by people, does not eat, grow or make more of itself, and does exactly one thing. A bacterium is alive, compares now with before, and makes more bacteria. Whether either 'thinks' depends on what we mean by thinking.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Good answers compare carefully.

items.p: Put these discoveries in time order, earliest first: all animals are made of cells (Schwann), Hooke names cells, every cell comes from a cell (Remak and Virchow), Leeuwenhoek sees living single cells.
items: all animals are made of cells (Schwann)
every cell comes from a cell (Remak and Virchow)
items.why: Hooke 1665, Leeuwenhoek 1674, Schwann 1839, Remak and Virchow in the 1850s. Science builds step by step.

items.p: Your body has about as many bacteria cells as human cells.
items.why: True. A careful 2016 count found roughly one bacterium for each human cell. The old saying of ten bacteria for each human cell was wrong.

items.p: Draw a model of a bacterium finding food by run and tumble. Use arrows for the runs and spirals for the tumbles.
items.a: Straight arrows that keep going when they head towards the food, and spirals then new arrows when they turn away, ending at the food.
items.why: A model drawing shows the hidden steps: run, check, keep or tumble.
items.art: A blank page with a dot of food in one corner and a tiny bacterium in the other.
items.context: Remember Run and Tumble, the game where you played a bacterium?

items.p: Your brain is made of cells, and single cells can sense, choose and remember. So where do you think thinking began?
items.a: Maybe thinking began with single cells sensing food and danger, billions of years ago. Brains came much later and are made of many cells signalling together. Scientists still argue about what to call thinking.
items.why: This is an open question. A good answer uses evidence from the unit.

opts: The smallest piece of a living thing that is alive by itself
quiz.why: A cell is the smallest living piece of a living thing. Picking 'battery' mixes up two meanings of the word 'cell'.

quiz.p: Which is NOT made of cells?
quiz.why: Glass was never alive, so it has no cells. The leaf, your skin and the mushroom are parts of living things. Picking 'mushroom' usually means thinking mushrooms are not alive, but they are fungi, made of cells.

quiz.p: Where do new cells come from?
quiz.why: Every cell comes from a cell. Picking 'mud' is the old, disproved idea of spontaneous generation.

quiz.p: The thin skin from inside an onion looked like long boxes under the magnifier. What were the boxes?
quiz.why: The boxes are cells, fitted together like bricks. Bubbles are round with thick dark edges.
quiz.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

quiz.p: Why can we see cells in onion skin but not in a thick slice of onion?
opts: The skin is only one cell thick, so light passes through
The thick slice has no cells
quiz.why: Light must pass through the sample for us to see the cells clearly. A thick slice has many layers piled up and blocks the light. Picking 'no cells' is wrong: the whole onion is made of cells.
quiz.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

quiz.p: How are cheek cells different from onion cells?
opts: Cheek cells have no stiff wall, so they are floppy and roundish
quiz.why: Animal cells have no cell wall. Both kinds have a nucleus. Picking 'no nucleus' usually means the stain was too faint to show it.
quiz.context: Remember the cheek cell experiment, where you scraped the inside of your cheek and looked at the cells?

quiz.p: A cotton kurta is made of…
opts: something that was never made of cells
quiz.why: Cotton fibres are long single cells from a cotton plant. They are dead now. Picking 'never cells' usually means thinking cloth was never alive.

quiz.p: A mustard seed is about 1 millimetre across. An onion cell is about a tenth of a millimetre. About how many onion cells fit across a mustard seed?
quiz.why: A tenth of a millimetre, ten times over, makes one millimetre. So about 10. Picking 1,000 is closer to the number of bacteria that would fit.
quiz.context: Remember the Size Ladder, where each step was 10 times smaller?

opts: comparing the smell now with a few seconds ago, and turning if it gets weaker
asking other bacteria for a map
quiz.why: A bacterium has no eyes. It remembers for a few seconds and compares. Picking 'eyes' gives it parts it doesn't have.
quiz.context: Remember Run and Tumble, the game where you played a bacterium?

quiz.p: Do scientists agree that single cells think?
opts: No. They agree on what cells do, but argue about calling it thinking
Yes, all scientists say cells think like us
Yes, because cells have tiny brains
No, because cells never do anything
quiz.why: Cells sense, choose and remember a little. Whether that counts as thinking is debated. Picking 'cells never do anything' ignores what bacteria, Stentor and slime moulds do.

quiz.p: Who first saw living single cells, in a drop of lake water, in 1674?
opts: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek, a cloth-seller in Delft
quiz.why: Leeuwenhoek made his own tiny lenses. Hooke named cells earlier, but he looked at dead cork.

quiz.p: Which is the best way to make a fair test of three magnifiers?
opts: Look at the same onion skin, in the same light, with each one
Use a different onion each time
Look at onion with one and cheek with another
Use the strongest light only for the best one
quiz.why: Change only the magnifier, keep everything else the same. Then any difference comes from the magnifier.
quiz.context: Remember the onion skin experiment, where you peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at it with a magnifier?

quiz.p: Bowl A of warm milk had a spoon of curd. Bowl C had a spoon of curd that was boiled first. Only bowl A set. Why?
opts: The heat killed the curd bacteria, so there were no living cells to multiply
Boiled curd is too hot for ever
Curd sets only in the morning
quiz.why: New cells come only from living cells. The living bacteria in bowl A split again and again and set the milk. In bowl C, boiling had killed them. Picking 'too hot for ever' misses that the curd had cooled before it went in.
quiz.context: Remember the curd bowls experiment, where you set three bowls of warm milk overnight?

applications: Doctors count blood cells under a microscope, in a blood test, to find out if someone is ill.
Labs look at cells from a swab or a tiny piece of skin to find diseases like cancer early.
Curd, idli, dosa, bread and dhokla are made with the help of living single cells: bacteria and yeast.
Farmers and plant scientists look at plant cells to breed better crops, as E.K. Janaki Ammal did with sugarcane.
Water testers look at drops of water under a microscope to check for harmful single cells.
Scientists grow skin cells in labs to help people with bad burns heal.
Engineers have used the rules a slime mould follows to help plan transport and computer networks.
Paper microscopes like the Foldscope let schools and village health workers see cells cheaply.
Police and forensic scientists find a person's cells, like cheek cells on a cup, to solve crimes.
Cotton, jute, wood and paper are all made from plant cell walls.

open_questions.q: How did the very first cell begin?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody was there, and no fossils of the first cells survive. Scientists test ideas in labs, like tiny fatty bubbles holding copying molecules, but no one has made a living cell from non-living matter.

open_questions.q: Can a single cell feel anything?
open_questions.why_open: We can see what a cell does, but not what, if anything, it is like to be that cell. Nobody knows how to test it.

open_questions.q: Should we call what a single cell does 'thinking'?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists agree cells sense, choose and remember a little. They disagree about where to draw the line for the word 'thinking'.

open_questions.q: How does a slime mould, with no brain, decide which tubes to keep?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have good models: tubes that carry more flow grow thicker, and the rest fade. But the full story of how one cell coordinates itself is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Could there be life on other worlds that is not made of cells?
open_questions.why_open: All life we know is made of cells. We have only ever studied life on Earth.

open_questions.q: How many kinds of single-celled life are there on Earth?
open_questions.why_open: Most have never been grown in a lab or named. Scientists find new ones in soil, seas and even clouds.

open_questions.q: Exactly how many cells are in your body right now?
open_questions.why_open: Careful estimates say about 30 trillion for a grown-up, but bodies differ and cells are always dying and being replaced.

maths.problem: In a phone photo of onion skin, Meera counted 10 cells side by side across 1 millimetre. How many cells would fit side by side across 1 centimetre? Remember, 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres.
maths.explain: 10 cells fit across 1 millimetre. 1 centimetre is 10 millimetres. So it is 10 groups of 10 cells. 10 times 10 is 100. So about 100 onion cells fit across 1 centimetre.
maths.context: This is about the onion skin experiment. You peeled the thin skin from inside an onion and looked at its cells with a magnifier.
maths.why_maths: Cells are too small to count across a whole onion. Counting a small part and multiplying lets scientists estimate big numbers.

maths.problem: In warm milk, a curd bacterium can split into two about once an hour. Start with 1 bacterium. How many will there be after 5 hours?
maths.explain: Every hour, each bacterium splits in two, so the number doubles. After 1 hour there are 2. After 2 hours, 4. After 3 hours, 8. After 4 hours, 16. After 5 hours, 32. A spoon of curd already holds billions of bacteria, so by morning there are far more.
maths.context: This is about the curd bowls experiment. You set warm milk with a spoon of curd overnight, and it turned into curd.
maths.why_maths: Doubling grows slowly at first and then very fast. The pattern shows why a few hours turn a spoon of curd into a whole bowl.

maths.problem: On the size ladder, each step is 10 times smaller. You are about 1 metre. An onion cell is 4 steps down. How many times smaller than you is an onion cell?
maths.explain: Each step is 10 times smaller. 4 steps is 10 times 10 times 10 times 10. 10 times 10 is 100. 100 times 10 is 1,000. 1,000 times 10 is 10,000. So an onion cell is about 10,000 times smaller than you.
maths.context: This is about the Size Ladder, where you drew steps from you down to a cell, each 10 times smaller.
maths.why_maths: Cells are so small that ordinary words like 'tiny' don't say how tiny. Multiplying tens shows exactly how far down the ladder they are.

maths.problem: A grown-up's body has about 30 trillion cells. A year has about 30 million seconds. If you counted one cell every second, day and night, about how many years would it take? Hint: 30 trillion is a million times 30 million.
maths.explain: Each year you could count about 30 million cells. 30 trillion is a million lots of 30 million. So it would take about a million years. (A year really has about 31.5 million seconds, so it is a little under a million years.)
maths.context: This is about the cheek cell experiment, where you looked at a few of your own cells, and the fact that a grown-up has about 30 trillion.
maths.why_maths: A number like 30 trillion is too big to picture. Turning it into time helps us feel how many cells we are made of.

maths.problem: In the Run and Tumble game, Dev took 12 runs to find the lemon. Each run was 3 steps. How many steps did Dev walk in all?
maths.explain: Dev took 12 runs of 3 steps each. 12 times 3 is 36. So Dev walked 36 steps, even though the lemon was much closer in a straight line. That is how a bacterium moves: lots of small tries.
maths.context: This is about Run and Tumble, the game where you played a bacterium finding food with your eyes shut, in runs of 3 steps.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying runs by steps shows how much extra a bacterium travels by trying and checking, compared with a straight line.
